title: MAHARASHTRA CLASS 12 — English | Verbs Tenses Present Past Future
description: Subject-wise test on Verbs Tenses Present Past Future (English) for MAHARASHTRA CLASS 12. 25Q.
subject: maha12-english
instructions: Topic: Verbs Tenses Present Past Future

questions.question: Which of the following options correctly completes the sentence: 'The Earth ______ around the Sun'?

options.explanation: The base form 'move' is incorrect because it does not agree with the singular subject 'Earth'. The correct form is 'moves'.
'Moved' is the past tense and does not fit the context of a universal truth.
The simple present tense 'moves' correctly describes the Earth's continuous movement around the Sun.
The present participle 'moving' cannot stand alone as a verb in this sentence.

questions.explanation: The Earth's movement around the Sun is a universal truth, which requires the simple present tense. 'Moves' is the correct form of the verb for this context.
questions.hint: Universal truths are expressed in the simple present tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'Look! The children ______ happily in the garden right now.'

options.explanation: The simple present tense 'play' does not indicate an action happening right now.
The past tense 'played' does not fit the context of an action happening now.
The present continuous tense 'are playing' correctly describes an action happening at the moment.
The present perfect tense 'have played' does not indicate an action happening right now.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'right now' indicates an action happening at the moment of speaking, which requires the present continuous tense. The correct form is 'are playing'.
questions.hint: Actions happening at the moment of speaking use the present continuous tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which option correctly completes the sentence: 'My family ______ to Nashik last summer for a vacation'?

options.explanation: The base form 'go' is incorrect because it does not indicate a past action.
The simple present tense 'goes' does not fit the context of a past action.
The simple past tense 'went' correctly describes a completed action in the past.
The present participle 'going' cannot stand alone as a verb in this sentence.

questions.explanation: 'Last summer' indicates a completed action in the past, which requires the simple past tense. The correct form is 'went'.
questions.hint: Completed actions in the past use the simple past tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Select the correct option to complete the sentence: 'I ______ my final board exam next month.'

options.explanation: The simple present tense 'write' does not indicate a future action.
The past tense 'wrote' does not fit the context of a future action.
The simple future tense 'will write' correctly describes a future action.
The present continuous tense 'am writing' can indicate a planned future but is less direct than 'will write'.

questions.explanation: 'Next month' indicates a future action, which is typically expressed using the simple future tense 'will write'.
questions.hint: Future actions are often expressed using the simple future tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'She ______ her wallet, so she cannot pay for the groceries now.'

options.explanation: The simple past tense 'lost' does not indicate a present relevance.
The simple present tense 'loses' does not indicate a past action.
The present perfect tense 'has lost' correctly describes a past action with present relevance.
The past perfect tense 'had lost' is incorrect because it does not indicate present relevance.

questions.explanation: The action of losing the wallet happened in the past, but its effect ('cannot pay now') is still relevant in the present. This requires the present perfect tense 'has lost'.
questions.hint: Actions with present relevance use the present perfect tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which option correctly completes the sentence: 'By the time the fire brigade arrived, the building ______ completely ______'?

options.explanation: The present perfect tense 'has burnt' is incorrect because it does not indicate a past action before another past action.
The past perfect tense 'had burnt' correctly describes an action completed before another past action.
The past continuous tense 'was burning' does not indicate completion before another past action.
The future tense 'will burn' is incorrect because it does not fit the context of past actions.

questions.explanation: The past perfect tense ('had burnt') is used to describe an action that happened before another action in the past ('the fire brigade arrived').
questions.hint: The past perfect tense is used for actions completed before another past action.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Select the correct option to complete the sentence: 'They ______ on this project since morning and still haven't finished.'

options.explanation: The simple past tense 'worked' does not indicate continuity in the present.
The present perfect continuous tense 'have been working' correctly describes an action started in the past and continuing now.
The present continuous tense 'are working' does not indicate an action that started in the past.
The future tense 'will work' does not fit the context of an action continuing from the past.

questions.explanation: The action started in the past ('since morning') and is still continuing in the present ('and still haven't finished'), which requires the present perfect continuous tense 'have been working'.
questions.hint: Actions that started in the past and continue in the present use the present perfect continuous tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'This time next year, I ______ my graduation ceremony.'

options.explanation: The simple present tense 'attend' does not indicate a future action in progress.
The simple future tense 'will attend' does not indicate an action in progress at a future time.
The future continuous tense 'will be attending' correctly describes an action in progress at a future time.
The future perfect tense 'will have attended' does not indicate an action in progress at a future time.

questions.explanation: 'This time next year' indicates an action that will be in progress at a specific point in the future, which requires the future continuous tense 'will be attending'.
questions.hint: Actions in progress at a specific future time use the future continuous tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Assertion (A): The sentence 'She has lived in Mumbai for ten years' correctly uses the Present Perfect tense. Reason (R): The Present Perfect tense is used to describe an action that began in the past and continues up to the present moment. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason is the correct explanation for the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both A and R are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: Both A and R are true.

questions.explanation: The assertion correctly uses the present perfect tense to show that living in Mumbai started in the past and continues now. The reason accurately defines the usage of the present perfect tense in such a context, thus explaining the assertion.
questions.hint: The present perfect tense describes actions that began in the past and continue to the present.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Read the following scenario and choose the best option to complete the sentences: 'Last night, while I ______ (read) a book, my phone suddenly ______ (ring). I picked it up and found that my friend ______ (call) to tell me about her new job.' Which option correctly fills the blanks in the given order?

options.explanation: The past continuous tense 'was reading' describes an action in progress. The simple past tense 'rang' describes an interrupting action. The past continuous tense 'was calling' describes an action in progress at the time of speaking in the past.
The simple past tense 'read' does not indicate an action in progress. The simple past tense 'called' does not describe an action in progress.
The past perfect tense 'had called' is incorrect because it does not describe an action in progress at the time of speaking in the past.
The simple past tense 'read' does not indicate an action in progress. The past continuous tense 'was ringing' is incorrect for the interrupting action.

questions.explanation: The first blank requires the past continuous tense ('was reading') to describe an action in progress when another action ('rang') occurred. The third blank requires the past continuous tense ('was calling') to describe an action in progress at the time of speaking in the past.
questions.hint: Use the past continuous tense for actions in progress and the simple past tense for actions that interrupt them.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which form of the verb correctly completes the sentence: 'While I ______ (read) a book, my phone suddenly ______ (ring)'?

options.explanation: Correct: 'was reading' (ongoing past action) and 'rang' (interrupting action).
Incorrect: 'read' is simple past, not continuous, for the ongoing action.
Incorrect: 'was ringing' suggests the phone was continuously ringing, which is not the case here.
Incorrect: Both verbs are in the wrong tense for the context.

questions.explanation: The first blank requires the past continuous tense ('was reading') to indicate an ongoing action in the past, while the second blank uses the simple past ('rang') for the action that interrupted it.
questions.hint: The first action is ongoing in the past, and the second is a sudden, completed action.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which tense correctly completes the sentence: 'My friend ______ (call) to tell me' in the context of the past actions?

options.explanation: Incorrect: 'called' is simple past, which does not convey the ongoing nature of the action.
Correct: 'was calling' indicates the ongoing or purposeful nature of the action in the past.
Incorrect: 'had called' is past perfect, which is not needed here as there is no earlier past action to reference.
Incorrect: 'calls' is present tense, which is not suitable for past context.

questions.explanation: The past continuous ('was calling') is used here because the action was ongoing at the time of the interruption (phone ringing) or was the reason for the call.
questions.hint: The verb describes an action that was happening at the same time as another past event.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: My sister usually ______ (read) a book before going to bed.

options.explanation: This is the base form of the verb, which is incorrect for a third-person singular subject in the Simple Present tense.
Correct. The verb takes an '-s' for a third-person singular subject in the Simple Present tense.
This is the Present Continuous tense, which is incorrect for a habitual action indicated by 'usually'.
This is the Simple Future tense, which is incorrect for a habitual action.

questions.explanation: The adverb 'usually' indicates a habitual action, which requires the Simple Present tense. For a third-person singular subject ('sister'), the verb takes an '-s'.
questions.hint: The adverb 'usually' suggests a routine action.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Identify the tense of the underlined verb in the sentence: 'The students *were preparing* for their final exams all last week.'

options.explanation: Simple Past would use the base form of the verb without 'were'.
Present Continuous uses 'am/is/are + verb-ing' and refers to the present.
Correct. The structure 'were preparing' indicates the Past Continuous tense.
Past Perfect uses 'had + past participle' and refers to an action completed before another past action.

questions.explanation: The structure 'were + verb-ing' indicates the Past Continuous tense, which describes an action that was ongoing over a period in the past.
questions.hint: Look for the auxiliary verb 'were' followed by the '-ing' form of the verb.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: If you hurry, you ______ (catch) the last bus to the city.

options.explanation: Simple Past tense is incorrect for a conditional sentence expressing a real possibility in the future.
This is an incorrect tense for a conditional sentence; it should be Simple Future.
Present Continuous tense is incorrect for a conditional sentence expressing a real possibility in the future.
Correct. Simple Future tense is required for the main clause in a Type 1 conditional sentence.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 1 conditional sentence (real possibility). The 'if' clause uses the Simple Present ('hurry'), so the main clause requires the Simple Future tense ('will catch').
questions.hint: Type 1 conditionals use 'if' + Simple Present in the first clause and Simple Future in the second.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: They ______ (live) in this house since 2010.

options.explanation: Present Continuous tense is incorrect for an action that started in the past and continues to the present.
Simple Past tense is incorrect for an action that continues up to the present.
Correct. Present Perfect tense is used for actions that started in the past and continue to the present.
Simple Future tense is incorrect for an action that started in the past.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'since 2010' indicates an action that started in the past and continues up to the present. This is a key indicator for the Present Perfect tense.
questions.hint: The word 'since' often indicates the use of the Present Perfect tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: While I ______ (watch) television, my phone suddenly ______ (ring).

options.explanation: Correct. Past Continuous ('was watching') describes the ongoing action, and Simple Past ('rang') describes the interruption.
Simple Past for both actions is incorrect for describing an ongoing action interrupted by another.
Both actions as Past Continuous is incorrect for describing an interruption.
Simple Past for the first action and Past Continuous for the second is incorrect for describing an interruption.

questions.explanation: The first blank describes an ongoing action in the past ('was watching'), which was interrupted by a shorter, completed action in the past ('rang'). This combination uses Past Continuous and Simple Past.
questions.hint: The first action is ongoing, while the second is a sudden interruption.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: By the time we reached the station, the train ______ (already depart).

options.explanation: Simple Past tense is incorrect for an action completed before another past action.
Correct. Past Perfect tense is used for an action completed before another past action.
Past Continuous tense is incorrect for an action completed before another past action.
Present Perfect tense is incorrect for an action completed before another past action.

questions.explanation: The action of the train departing happened before another past action (reaching the station). To indicate an action completed before another past action, the Past Perfect tense is used.
questions.hint: The phrase 'by the time' often indicates the use of the Past Perfect tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: By next month, I ______ (work) on this project for five years.

options.explanation: Simple Future tense is incorrect for emphasizing duration up to a future point.
Future Continuous tense is incorrect for emphasizing duration up to a future point.
Correct. Future Perfect Continuous tense is used for an action continuing up to a future point with emphasis on duration.
Present Perfect tense is incorrect for a future point.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes an action that will continue up to a specific future point ('next month') and emphasizes its duration ('for five years'). This requires the Future Perfect Continuous tense.
questions.hint: The phrase 'by next month' and 'for five years' indicate the use of the Future Perfect Continuous tense.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** The sentence 'She has been teaching English for ten years' correctly uses the Present Perfect Continuous tense. **Reason (R):** The Present Perfect Continuous tense is used to describe an action that began in the past, continues into the present, and often implies that the action might continue into the future, emphasizing its duration.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Correct. The assertion is true, and the reason correctly explains it.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and the reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: The assertion is true.

questions.explanation: The assertion correctly identifies the tense. The reason accurately defines the usage of the Present Perfect Continuous tense, specifically mentioning its application for actions that started in the past, continue to the present, and highlight duration, thus perfectly explaining the assertion.
questions.hint: Check if the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Read the following dialogue: 'I'm sorry I'm late,' said Mark. 'My car ______ (break down) on the highway, and I ______ (wait) for a tow truck for an hour before I ______ (get) a ride.' Choose the correct sequence of tenses to fill in the blanks.

options.explanation: Incorrect sequence. The first action should be in Past Perfect.
Incorrect sequence. The second action should be in Past Perfect Continuous.

options.text: had broken down, had been waiting, got
options.explanation: Correct. The sequence uses Past Perfect, Past Perfect Continuous, and Simple Past.
Incorrect sequence. The first action should be in Past Perfect.

questions.explanation: Mark's car breaking down happened before he started waiting, so 'had broken down' (Past Perfect). The waiting for a tow truck was an ongoing action for a duration before he got a ride, so 'had been waiting' (Past Perfect Continuous). Finally, getting a ride is a simple past completed action after the waiting, so 'got' (Simple Past).
questions.hint: The first action happened before the second, and the third action is a simple past completion.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Look at the forecast: 'The weather bureau predicts that by noon tomorrow, the rain ______ (stop) and the sun ______ (shine) brightly. However, strong winds ______ (continue) throughout the day.' Choose the correct sequence of tenses for the verbs in parentheses.

options.text: will stop, will shine, will continue
options.explanation: Incorrect sequence. The first action should be in Future Perfect.

options.text: will have stopped, will be shining, will continue
options.explanation: Correct sequence. The tenses match the actions described.

options.text: will stop, will be shining, will be continuing
options.explanation: Incorrect sequence. The first action should be in Future Perfect.

options.text: will have stopped, will shine, will be continuing
options.explanation: Incorrect sequence. The second action should be in Future Continuous.

questions.explanation: 'By noon tomorrow' indicates an action completed before a future point, so 'will have stopped' (Future Perfect). The sun will be shining *at* that future point, indicating an ongoing future action, so 'will be shining' (Future Continuous). The strong winds are predicted to continue as a general future action, so 'will continue' (Simple Future).
questions.hint: The first action is completed before a future point, the second is ongoing at that point, and the third is a general future action.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which option correctly completes the sentence? I ______ my lunch just now, so I'm not hungry anymore.

options.explanation: Simple past tense 'ate' does not indicate a connection to the present state of not being hungry.
Present Perfect tense 'have eaten' correctly indicates a recent action with a present consequence.
Past Perfect tense 'had eaten' is used for actions completed before another past action, which is not the case here.
Present Continuous tense 'am eating' indicates an action happening now, not a completed action.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'just now' indicates a very recent past action, and the consequence ('so I'm not hungry anymore') is relevant in the present. This situation calls for the Present Perfect tense, which connects a past action to the present.
questions.hint: Consider the use of the Present Perfect tense for actions that happened at an unspecified time before now and have a connection to the present.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the sequence of tenses?

options.text: She said that she has visited Paris last year.
options.explanation: Incorrect use of present perfect tense with 'last year' in reported speech after a past tense verb.

options.text: If I would have known, I would have come.
options.explanation: Incorrect structure for a third conditional sentence; should be 'If I had known, I would have come.'

options.text: He told me that he had finished his assignment before the deadline.
options.explanation: Correct use of past perfect tense 'had finished' to indicate an action completed before another past action.

options.text: We will go to the park if it will not rain.
options.explanation: Incorrect use of future tense in the 'if' clause; should be 'if it does not rain'.

questions.explanation: A) Incorrect because 'said' (past tense) requires the reported speech to be in a past tense form (e.g., 'had visited' or 'visited'), not present perfect. B) Incorrect because it uses 'would have known' instead of 'had known' in a third conditional structure. C) Correct because 'told' is in the simple past tense, and 'had finished' correctly indicates an action completed before another past action. D) Incorrect because in a first conditional sentence, the 'if' clause uses the simple present tense, not future.
questions.hint: Remember that the sequence of tenses requires maintaining consistency in time references within a sentence.
questions.subject: maha12-english

questions.question: Select the most appropriate tense for the blank: By the end of this year, Professor Sharma ______ at this university for twenty years.

options.explanation: Simple Future tense 'will teach' does not indicate completion of the twenty-year duration by the specified future time.
Future Perfect tense 'will have taught' correctly indicates the completion of a twenty-year duration by the end of this year.
Future Perfect Continuous tense 'will have been teaching' emphasizes the ongoing nature of the action but is less common in such contexts for board exams.
Present Perfect tense 'has taught' does not fit the future time reference 'By the end of this year'.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'By the end of this year' indicates a specific point in the future. 'for twenty years' specifies a duration that will be completed by that future point. The Future Perfect tense ('will have taught') is used to express an action that will be completed or will have reached a certain duration by a specific time in the future.
questions.hint: Consider the use of the Future Perfect tense for actions that will be completed by a specific time in the future.
questions.subject: maha12-english
